Q: How do I get logs from Sonos apps/devices? A:

The closest thing you can do to get the logs is to subscribe to the all the namespaces. Both the SOAP (SMAPI) and Control (REST) APIs have Subscribe functionality for each Namespace.

Example:

https://docs.sonos.com/reference/playback-subscribe-groupid

It maybe that I've returned some invalid data, but from the service's point of view the HTTP request/response was completed with a HTTP 200.

When I am developing Request/Response-base code, I keep each response so I can easily debug and troubleshoot.

So instead of doing something like this:

# API Call #1
response = requests.post(url, headers=headers)
# API Call #2
response = requests.post(url, headers=headers)

You could do something like this:

# API Call #1
r1 = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=json.dumps(data))
# API Call #2
r2 = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=json.dumps(data))

You could store each of those responses in a dictionary or list, so you can go back through them to debug.

Another option, is the ugly, but "effective" verbose method:

# Ugly But Effective
r1 = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=json.dumps(data))
print(r1)
print(r1.status_code)
print(r1.json())
print(r1.request.body)
print(r1.request.headers)

Q: How to read the value of a widget's padding option A:

After inspecting the "pixel objects", as well as the different return values due to different versions, my current workaround is to parse the return value as follows:

def get_padding_quartet(widget):
    """Get left, top, right, bottom padding values

    Some widgets feature a padding option. Setting the option works
    by providing an integer value or a sequence of integer values.
    However, when reading the option, the return value might have a
    custom format and needs to be parsed, in order to get its four
    integer pixel values for left, top, right and bottom padding.

    Example:

        >>> widget.configure(padding=(100, 50))
        >>> widget.configure("padding")
        ('padding', 'padding', 'Pad', '', (<pixel object: '100'>, <pixel object: '50'>))

    Depending on the version, might also look like this:

        >>> widget.configure(padding=(100, 50))
        >>> widget.configure("padding")
        ('padding', 'padding', 'Pad', '', (100, 50))

    Also supports non-integer, non-pixel values:

        >>> widget.configure(padding=("2c", "1c"))
        >>> widget.configure("padding")
        ('padding', 'padding', 'Pad', '', (<pixel object at 0x1e99d80>, <pixel object at 0x1e9d2f0>))

    > The string representation is a list of up to four length
    > specifications “left top right bottom”. If fewer than four
    > elements are specified, bottom defaults to top, right
    > defaults to left, and top defaults to left.

    Source: https://www.tcl-lang.org/man/tcl8.7/TkLib/ttk_Geometry.html#M7
    """
    padding = widget.configure("padding")[-1]
    if not padding:
        converter = lambda value: 0
    elif isinstance(padding[0], int):
        converter = lambda value: value
    else:
        converter = lambda value: int(widget.winfo_fpixels(value.string))
    values = map(converter, padding)
    left, top, right, bottom, *_ = [*values, None, None, None, None]
    left = 0 if left is None else left
    top = left if top is None else top
    right = left if right is None else right
    bottom = top if bottom is None else bottom
    return left, top, right, bottom

Using the example from above:

label.configure(padding=(100, 50))
print(get_padding_quartet(label))

This would print:

(100, 50, 100, 50)

Q: Refactoring C# CSV parser and data aggregation: Best practices for Dictionary sorting and culture-specific parsing A:

The use of Convert.ToDouble(sor2[6].Replace('.', ',')); suggests to me that the Current Culture of your program expects a decimal comma, but the input file uses a decimal point.

However there is no need to do such a Replace(). You should be able to use this instead, which parses using a culture that expects a decimal point:

AtlagosJegyar = double.Parse(s, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);

Or if you know what culture was used to generate the file (e.g. en-US) then you can specify it by name for even more certainty of using the right parsing settings:

AtlagosJegyar = double.Parse(s, new CultureInfo("en-US"));
